title: From the GX-1 to the CS-80
intro: The CS-80 was Yamaha’s flagship synthesizer of the late 1970s, at the top of the CS series of 1977 beside the smaller CS-50 and CS-60. It followed the organ-sized GX-1, with which it shares two oscillators per voice, a keyboard that answers to pressure as well as velocity, and a ribbon. Each of its eight notes plays two complete channels at once, which gives it its famously rich sound.

timeline.name: Yamaha GX-1
timeline.text: Yamaha’s first polyphonic synthesizer, built into an organ console: two eight-voice keyboards of two oscillators per voice, a solo keyboard with a ribbon, a pedalboard and a keyboard that responds to pressure. Fewer than a hundred were made.

timeline.name: Yamaha CS-60
timeline.text: An eight-voice polysynth of one oscillator per voice, with the same resonant high-pass and low-pass filters and a 61-key keyboard: a smaller CS-80 without its second channel and its pressure-sensitive keys.

timeline.name: Yamaha CS-80
timeline.text: Eight notes of two channels each, every channel a VCO giving square, sawtooth and sine, a high-pass and a low-pass filter moved by the IL-AL-A-D-R envelope, and a VCA. Twenty-two presets, four memories, a keyboard that senses velocity and pressure on each key, a ribbon, a sub oscillator, a ring modulator and a stereo tremolo/chorus. It weighs about 100 kg.

relatives.name: Yamaha CS-50
relatives.text: The smallest of the three CS polysynths: four voices, with a simpler panel than the CS-80.

relatives.name: Arturia CS-80V
relatives.text: A software recreation of the CS-80 for computers, which brought its sound to many players who would never own the hardware.

relatives.name: Black Corporation Deckard’s Dream
relatives.text: An eight-voice analogue polysynth modelled on the CS-80, with two layers per voice and polyphonic aftertouch, in a rack-style case.

note: The CS-80 was in many studios of the late 1970s and early 1980s, but which synth played which part is often not documented. Only records where the CS-80’s part is widely reported are listed; the other sounds here are general techniques.
